Booklet A identifies the option/question permutation, not a separate session; set/session stays blank. The physical filename 2012.pdf is preserved. All 20 source pages are present, including three final rough-work pages.

Source page 1 specifies three hours, 65 single-answer objective questions and 100 marks. Q1-25 carry one mark and Q26-55 two marks. General Aptitude is Q56-65, with five one-mark and five two-mark questions: ten questions totaling 15 marks.

Original navigation blocks: one-mark technical Q1-25; two-mark technical Q26-47; common data Q48-51; linked pairs Q52-55; General Aptitude Q56-65. Attempt all; no optional-section limits, descriptive answers, NAT or MSQ in this paper.

All 65 entries have authored worked references and comparison with a downloaded historical booklet-A key. All 65 key entries agree with the indexed IIT Kanpur official GATE archive. The official archive host could not be downloaded directly (DNS/502); the locally retained PDF is a gatecse.in mirror and is not labeled an authenticated original download. Seventeen supplied Made Easy key entries and eleven relevant discussion pages/indexed discussions were checked separately; remaining discussion links are cache mappings.

The historical booklet-A key awards Marks to All for Q3, Q29, Q38, Q39, Q45 and Q60 (10 marks). This practice implements that wording as full marks for every candidate, including blanks. Question copies have independent IDs and keys, complete source-page provenance and independent diagram files. Original book records, prior papers and existing attempts are preserved. This dataset is excluded from book-based subject and weighted mocks.

questions.text:
Consider the following logical inferences.
$I_1$: If it rains then the cricket match will not be played.
The cricket match was played.
Inference: There was no rain.
$I_2$: If it rains then the cricket match will not be played.
It did not rain.
Inference: The cricket match was played.
Which of the following is TRUE?
questions.optB: $I_1$ is correct but $I_2$ is not a correct inference
questions.optC: $I_1$ is not correct but $I_2$ is a correct inference
questions.optD: Both $I_1$ and $I_2$ are not correct inferences
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer:
Let $R$ mean rain and $M$ mean the match is played. The premise is $R\Rightarrow
eg M$. From $M$ its contrapositive gives $
eg R$, so I1 is valid. From $
eg R$ nothing forces $M$: another cause could cancel the match. I2 denies the antecedent and is invalid.

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE?
questions.optA: Every relation in 3NF is also in BCNF
questions.optB: A relation R is in 3NF if every non-prime attribute of R is fully functionally dependent on every key of R
questions.optC: Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF
questions.optD: No relation can be in both BCNF and 3NF
questions.subject: 12. DBMS
questions.referenceAnswer: BCNF requires the determinant of every nontrivial functional dependency to be a superkey. This implies 3NF, whose alternative permits a prime attribute on the right. The reverse implication fails. Full dependence of non-prime attributes on candidate keys alone is a 2NF condition, not a sufficient 3NF test.

questions.text: Assuming $P\ne NP$, which of the following is TRUE?
questions.referenceAnswer: If any NP-complete problem were in P, polynomial reductions to it would put every NP problem in P. Under $P\ne NP$, the intersection of P and NP-complete is therefore empty. NP-hard also contains problems outside NP, and P cannot equal the NP-complete class under the given assumption.

questions.text: What is the complement of the language accepted by the NFA shown below? Assume $\Sigma = \{a\}$ and $\epsilon$ is the empty string. [IMG_1]
questions.subject: 2. TOC
questions.referenceAnswer: The initial state is nonaccepting, so epsilon is rejected. One a reaches the accepting middle state; two epsilon moves then return to the start, allowing the same cycle to repeat. Thus every positive-length string over the unary alphabet is accepted: the language is $a^+$. Its complement in $\{a\}^*$ is $\{\varepsilon\}$.

questions.text:
What is the correct translation of the following statement into mathematical logic?
"Some real numbers are rational"
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: Some means existential quantification, and the same witness must be both real and rational. Hence $\exists x(\operatorname{real}(x)\land\operatorname{rational}(x))$. A disjunction does not require both properties; a universal implication expresses a different claim.

questions.text: Given the basic ER and relational models, which of the following is INCORRECT?

questions.optB: An attribute of an entity can be composite
questions.optC: In a row of a relational table, an attribute can have more than one value
questions.optD: In a row of a relational table, an attribute can have exactly one value or a NULL value
questions.subject: 12. DBMS
questions.referenceAnswer: The basic ER model allows multivalued and composite attributes. In the basic relational model, each cell holds one atomic value (or a NULL marker in the question's convention), so a row attribute cannot contain several values. Therefore statement C is the incorrect statement.

questions.text:
Which of the following statements are TRUE about an SQL query?
P: An SQL query can contain a HAVING clause even if it does not have a GROUP BY clause
Q: An SQL query can contain a HAVING clause only if it has a GROUP BY clause
R: All attributes used in the GROUP BY clause must appear in the SELECT clause
S: Not all attributes used in the GROUP BY clause need to appear in the SELECT clause
questions.subject: 12. DBMS
questions.referenceAnswer: Published key C says Q and R; the supplied book retains that historical key. Under SQL semantics, however, HAVING can filter one implicit group without GROUP BY, and a grouping column need not be projected: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM T GROUP BY department is a counterexample to R. Thus P and S give B. The discussion explicitly records this conflict. No single interpretation is silently forced: the historical key is retained as provenance and this item is self-assessed after submission.

questions.subject: 7. Algorithms

questions.text: Let G be a simple undirected planar graph on 10 vertices with 15 edges. If G is a connected graph, then the number of bounded faces in any embedding of G on the plane is equal to
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: Euler's formula for a connected plane graph is $V-E+F=2$, including the unbounded face. Thus $F=2-10+15=7$. Subtracting the unbounded face gives six bounded faces.

questions.text: Let $W(n)$ and $A(n)$ denote respectively, the worst case and average case running time of an algorithm executed on an input of size $n$. Which of the following is ALWAYS TRUE?
questions.subject: 7. Algorithms
questions.referenceAnswer: For every input size the average cost is no greater than the largest cost over the same inputs. Therefore $A(n)\le W(n)$ and $A(n)=O(W(n))$. Equality of order need not hold, while little-o is not guaranteed because average and worst costs can coincide.

questions.text: Which of the following problems are decidable? 1) Does a given program ever produce an output? 2) If $L$ is a context-free language, then, is $\bar{L}$ also context-free? 3) If $L$ is a regular language, then, is $\bar{L}$ also regular? 4) If $L$ is a recursive language, then, is $\bar{L}$ also recursive?
questions.subject: 2. TOC
questions.referenceAnswer: Regular and recursive languages are closed under complement, making statements 3 and 4 always yes under their promises. Whether an arbitrary program ever outputs anything is undecidable by a halting reduction. Determining whether the complement of an arbitrary context-free language is itself context-free is also undecidable; nonclosure alone is not a proof of that undecidability. Only 3 and 4 are decidable.

questions.text:
Given the language $L=\{ab,aa,baa\}$, which of the following strings are in $L^*$?
1) abaabaaabaa
2) aaaabaaaa
3) baaaaabaaaab
4) baaaaabaa
questions.subject: 2. TOC
questions.referenceAnswer: Membership in $L^*$ means complete concatenation of words ab, aa and baa. Valid splits are 1: ab|aa|baa|ab|aa; 2: aa|aa|baa|aa; 4: baa|aa|baa. A prefix dynamic-programming check cannot completely consume string 3, baaaaabaaaab. Hence 1, 2 and 4 are members.

questions.optB: a schedule that is not conflict serializable

questions.text: The bisection method is applied to compute a zero of the function $f(x)=x^4-x^3-x^2-4$ in the interval $[1,9]$. The method converges to a solution after ______ iterations.
questions.referenceAnswer: The successive midpoints are 5, 3 and 2. Values are $f(5)=471>0$, $f(3)=41>0$, $f(1)=-5<0$ and $f(2)=0$. Bisection therefore finds an exact root at the third midpoint; no tolerance assumption is needed.

questions.text: Let $G$ be a weighted graph with edge weights greater than one and $G'$ be the graph constructed by squaring the weights of edge in $G$. Let $T$ and $T'$ be the minimum spanning trees of $G$ and $G'$ respectively, with total weights $t$ and $t'$. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.subject: 7. Algorithms
questions.referenceAnswer: Historical key: Marks to All. Squaring positive weights preserves their order, so the family of MST edge sets is preserved; a consistent tie-breaking rule can select the same tree. With at least two tree edges, $\sum w_i^2<(\sum w_i)^2$ because all cross products are positive, suggesting B. But for a two-vertex, single-edge graph equality holds, and ties can also yield distinct chosen trees. The unqualified wording omits these conditions. The published all-candidate award, rather than a forced option, gives two marks even for a blank response.

questions.text:
What is the minimal form of the Karnaugh map shown below? Assume that X denotes a don't care term.
$$\begin{array}{c|cccc} cd\backslash ab&00&01&11&10\\\hline 00&1&X&X&1\\\hline 01&X&\phantom{0}&\phantom{0}&1\\\hline 11&\phantom{0}&\phantom{0}&\phantom{0}&\phantom{0}\\\hline 10&1&\phantom{0}&\phantom{0}&X\\\hline\end{array}$$
questions.optD: $\overline b\,\overline d+\overline b\,\overline c+\overline c\,\overline d$

questions.referenceAnswer: Blank K-map cells are zeros and X cells are don't-cares. A wraparound group covering rows cd=00,10 and columns ab=00,10 yields $\overline b\,\overline d$. A misses the 1 at ab=10, cd=01; C is an unreduced equivalent cover; D has an unnecessary term. The minimal expression is B.

questions.text: Suppose a fair six-sided die is rolled once. If the value on the die is 1, 2 or 3 then the die is rolled a second time. What is the probability that the sum total of values that turn up is at least 6?
questions.subject: 11. Engg. Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: If the first roll is 6, success has probability $1/6$. If it is 1, 2 or 3, the second roll must be respectively at least 5, 4 or 3, yielding 2, 3 and 4 successful faces. Total probability is $1/6+(2+3+4)/36=15/36=5/12$. First rolls 4 and 5 stop unsuccessfully.
